title: Two doubts answer the two trusts: deadly doubt of the promise versus non-mortal doubt of one’s own faith
source_text: XXV. Atque ut res magis illustretur, ab iisdem Viris Doctis recte observatum est, duplici isti fiduciae, duplicem opponi dubitationem, & haesitationem. Unam qua quis dubitat circa Dei promissiones, an scilicet, verae sint, necne; & an debeat quaerere in Deo perfugium, & salutem in Christo. Alteram vero qua quis de veritate divinae promissionis minime dubitans, & certus ad Deum confugere, ac salutem in Christo quaerere, de propria tamen salute & peccatorum suorum remissione dubitat, ex propriae suae infirmitatis sensu; & quia concussus tentationibus, non videtur fidem satis firmam in se agnoscere, ut nec fructus satis poenitentia dignos. Prior illa dubitatio perniciosa & mortifera est, & cum fidei natura & veritate simpliciter pugnat. Posterior non item. Etenim quamvis fides perfecta illam expellat, ex quodam fidei defectu, & quasi morbo nascatur; cum fide tamen vera, licet infirma atque languida, consistere potest. Et dum fidei morbum quendam arguit, simul tamen est fidei adhuc vivae, necdum mortuae, argumentum. Quod dicit Jacobus, Epist. cap. 1. Eum qui dubitat a Domino expectare debere, de priori dubitatione intelligendum est, non de posteriori.
pass_a_gloss: And that the matter may be clearer, the same learned men have rightly observed that to that twofold trust a twofold doubt and hesitation is opposed. One by which someone doubts concerning God’s promises—whether they are true or not, and whether he ought to seek refuge in God and salvation in Christ. The other by which someone, not at all doubting the truth of the divine promise and certain that he ought to flee to God and seek salvation in Christ, yet doubts concerning his own salvation and the remission of his sins from a sense of his own infirmity, and because shaken by temptations he does not seem to recognize in himself faith firm enough, nor fruits worthy enough of repentance. The former doubt is pernicious and deadly and simply fights with the nature and truth of faith. The latter does not. For although perfect faith expels it, and it is born from a certain defect and as it were disease of faith, yet it can stand with true faith, though weak and languid. And while it argues a certain disease of faith, it is at the same time an argument of faith still living and not yet dead. What James says (Epistle ch. 1) that he who doubts ought not to expect anything from the Lord is to be understood of the former doubt, not the latter.
pass_b_english: Doubt of the promise’s truth kills faith; doubt of one’s own interest, born of sensed weakness, can coexist with true though languid faith.
James 1’s warning targets the first doubt, not the second.
